questions.q: Applying the four-question method to the capstone's portfolio-risk VQE project, which pattern does it fall under and why?
options: Pattern B, because ground-state energy estimation always requires fault-tolerant qubits
Neither pattern applies, since this isn't a quantum-shaped problem
Pattern B (whole program), because the result comes from a single circuit execution with no classical loop
Pattern A (coprocessor), because a classical optimizer iteratively drives an ansatz circuit, evaluating a Hamiltonian expectation value each iteration
questions.explain: The variational loop structure -- a classical optimizer iteratively evaluating a Hamiltonian expectation via the QPU -- is the textbook Pattern A case, same as the drug-discovery example from Chapter 1's lab.

questions.q: For the 6-parameter ansatz targeting 80 iterations with parameter-shift gradients, how many total circuit evaluations does the project require?
options: 80, one evaluation per iteration
480, computed as 6 x 80
13, the per-iteration evaluation count only
1,040, computed as (6x2+1) x 80 = 13 x 80
questions.explain: Each iteration needs 2 evaluations per parameter plus 1 for the cost itself: (6x2)+1=13. Across 80 iterations: 13x80=1,040 total circuit evaluations.

questions.q: The lesson computes a single daily run cost of $960.00. Why does it flag the monthly figure (~$21,120) as a potentially project-changing number?
options: Because the daily cost is irrelevant and only matters if multiplied by 1,000

Because if the real plan is to run this every single business day, the monthly cost (~22 x $960) could change a go/no-go decision, and it's better to surface that before writing any orchestration code
Because $960 is actually the monthly cost, not the daily cost
Because cloud providers refuse single-run costs above $500
questions.explain: Multiplying the per-run cost by the actual run frequency (22 business days) surfaces a much larger monthly commitment that a stakeholder should see and approve BEFORE implementation, not discover after the fact.

questions.q: Why does the lesson explicitly avoid making 'the quantum result beats a classical baseline' one of the capstone's success criteria?
options: Quantum advantage is often not achievable with today's hardware, and isn't what the capstone is actually testing -- the criteria instead focus on classical engineering quality (orchestration correctness, cost/latency tracking, reported standard error, operational observability)
Quantum advantage is guaranteed for this specific problem, so it isn't worth testing
Success criteria should never be stated explicitly in any project brief
Classical baselines are impossible to compute for any molecular system
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly reframes success around the classical engineering discipline the course teaches -- orchestration correctness, cost/latency tracking, and result observability -- rather than an often-unachievable quantum-advantage claim.

questions.q: What four things does the lesson say a reviewable one-page project brief should state?
options: The problem, the pattern (A or B), the architecture (ansatz/gradient method/batching/backend), the budget, and the success criteria
Only the final cost figure, with no other context
Only the names of team members assigned to the project
A full implementation of the orchestration code, written before any review happens
questions.explain: The brief described in the lesson covers problem statement, pattern classification, architecture specifics, budget (with monthly-cost flagging), and explicit engineering success criteria -- enough for a reviewer to approve or reject in one read.
